To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
reductions in healthcare spending were not associated with magnitude of recessions or debt crises, but were significantly correlated with exposure to IMF lending and tax revenue declines.

(1) healthcare expenditure in EU member states has been affected by the Great Recession, (2) the magnitude of the effect is associated with exposure to IMF loans, (3) tax revenue falls, but not underlying economic conditions, are the most significant determinants of healthcare expenditure change, (4) the political ideology of the ruling party is unrelated to healthcare expenditure change.
the magnitude of economic recesssion, debt crises, and the ideological orientation of the ruling political party are not associated with healthcare spending reductions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the political and economic determinants of healthcare spending.
the political economy of austerity in Europe and its implications for the financing of health care.
the political economy of austerity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the austerity measures imposed in the aftermath of the Great Recession were not driven by underlying economic conditions, but rather by political decisions to cut spending and by the influence of international financial institutions.
the political economy of austerity is the most important determinant of recent changes in health expenditure.
austerity policies, in the form of cuts to tax revenue, have been the primary drivers of healthcare expenditure change in recent years.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the austerity policies of international financial institutions have a disproportionate impact on health spending, and that this impact is not mitigated by the ideology of the governing parties or the severity of economic recessions.

healthcare expenditure changes in EU member states are more closely related to political and economic factors, such as tax revenue and international lending, than to the underlying economic conditions of recession or debt.
healthcare expenditure changes are not primarily driven by underlying macroeconomic conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IMF and the World Bank, which are often portrayed as neutral arbiters of financial policy, have a significant effect on healthcare budgets.
the austerity agenda of the IMF, European Union and national governments is having a disproportionate effect on healthcare spending.
the austerity measures imposed in many European countries have had an important impact on healthcare budgets.
